lessons.title: Eating outdoors (Ordering food)
objectives: Order food and drinks politely in a restaurant.
Use: Can/May I help you? I’d like… Would you like…?
lessons.intro: I ask: “You are in a restaurant and you are hungry. What do you say to the waiter?” Then we read the dialogue between Houda, Yahya and the waiter.
lessons.summary: Houda and her brother Yahya are eating out. The waiter asks: “Can I help you?” Houda says: “I’d like some lunch.” They order a starter (a little salad, a little soup), a main course (rice and fish, a vegetarian sandwich) and drinks (milk). At the end, Houda asks for the bill. To order we use: I would like… / I’d like… / I’ll have… The waiter asks: Would you like a starter? What would you like for the main course? Would you like anything to drink?
points: Waiter: Can I help you? / May I help you?
Customer: I’d like… / I’ll have…
Waiter: Would you like a starter / anything to drink?
Customer: Could you give us the bill, please?
Menu: starter, main course, dessert, drink.

application.q: Complete: Waiter: What would you like for the main course? – You: ____
application.a: I’d like a plate of rice and fish, please.

lines: Can I help you? – Yes, please.
I’d like some lunch, please.
I’ll have a vegetarian sandwich.
Would you like a starter?
What would you like for the main course?
Would you like anything to drink?
starter – main course – dessert – drink
Complete: Waiter: What would you like for the main course? – You: ____

lessons.title: Can I borrow your textbook? (Requests)
lessons.intro: I ask a student: “Can I borrow your pen?” He answers. Then I ask: “What did I ask for? Was I polite?”
lessons.summary: Aly forgot his English book at home. He asks his classmate Sidi: “Can I borrow your book?” Sidi is using it, so Aly asks the teacher: “Could you, please, lend me your book for a while?” To make a request we use: Can/Could I + base verb…? Can/Could you + base verb…? May I…? Will/Would you…? Do/Would you mind + verb-ing…? Could, May, Would you mind and I wonder if… are more formal than Can and Will.
points: Can/Could I + base verb…? (Can I borrow your book?)
Can/Could you + base verb…?
May I…? (May I use your ruler?)
Do/Would you mind + verb-ing…? → answer “No, not at all.” to accept.
Accept: Sure! / Of course! Decline: Sorry, I can’t.

application.q: Complete: ____ you mind opening the window? – No, not at all.
application.a: Would you mind opening the window? (or: Do you mind…)

lines: Can/Could I + verb? – Can I borrow your book?
Can/Could you + verb? – Could you lend me your pen?
May I + verb? – May I sit here?
Do/Would you mind + verb-ing? – Would you mind opening the window?
Accept: Sure! / Of course! / No, not at all.
Decline: Sorry, I can’t. I’m using it.
Complete: ____ you mind opening the window? – No, not at all.

lessons.title: At the food market (Quantity and prices)
match: Expressing and asking about quantity using quantifiers (many, much, a lot of, few, a few, little, a little…)
objectives: Ask for and give the price of items.
lessons.intro: I show a shopping list and ask: “How much sugar do we need? How many kilos of onions?”
lessons.summary: Aicha’s grandmother is at the market. She buys a 25 kg bag of rice, 5 kilos of sugar, a 5-liter bottle of cooking oil, 5 kilos of onions and 3 kilos of potatoes. She asks: “How much is all that?” The salesperson says: “That’s 2110 MRU.” We use How many with countable nouns (How many kilos?) and How much with uncountable nouns (How much sugar?). Many and much are for big amounts; few/a few (countable) and little/a little (uncountable) are for small amounts. To ask the price: How much is it? How much does it cost?
points: How many + countable noun: How many kilos?
How much + uncountable noun: How much sugar?
a few (countable), a little (uncountable).
Price: How much is it? How much does it cost? – It’s 2110 MRU.
Containers: a bag of, a bottle of, a kilo of, a packet of.

application.q: Complete with many or much: How ____ eggs are there in your fridge? How ____ salt is there?
application.a: How many eggs…? How much salt…?

lines: How many + countable: How many kilos do you want?
How much + uncountable: How much sugar did she buy?
a few + countable / a little + uncountable
How much is it? / How much does it cost?
That’s 2110 MRU.
a bag of rice – a bottle of oil – a kilo of sugar – a packet of tea
Complete with many or much: How ____ eggs are there in your fridge? How ____ salt is there?

lessons.title: Fruits and vegetables (Comparison)
match: Comparing people and things using short and long adjectives
objectives: Use the comparative of superiority, inferiority and equality.
lessons.intro: I show a date and a carrot and ask: “Which is sweeter? Which is cheaper?”
lessons.summary: The text compares fruits and vegetables: fruits are usually tastier than vegetables; dates are more delicious than carrots; vegetables are cheaper than fruits; sweet potatoes are as sweet as beetroots. Comparative of superiority: short adjective + -er + than (bigger than), more + long adjective + than (more delicious than). Irregular: good → better, bad → worse. Comparative of inferiority: less + adjective + than. Comparative of equality: as + adjective + as.
points: Short adjective + -er + than: tastier, bigger.
more + long adjective + than: more delicious.
Irregular: good → better, bad → worse.
Inferiority: less + adjective + than.
Equality: as + adjective + as.

application.q: Give the comparative: Watermelons are (big) melons. Plums are (tasty – equality) pineapples.
application.a: Watermelons are bigger than melons. Plums are as tasty as pineapples.

lines: short adj + -er + than: big → bigger than
more + long adj + than: more delicious than
good → better / bad → worse
less + adj + than: less tasty than
as + adj + as: as sweet as
big → bigger (CVC)
easy → easier (y → i)
Give the comparative: Watermelons are (big) melons. Plums are (tasty – equality) pineapples.
